content.text:
## Bottom line

**This is a good, market-credible offer—but not a compelling “leave a job you like” offer.**

I would:

1. **Not accept as-is.**
2. **Negotiate aggressively but professionally.**
3. **Stay at Meta if Google cannot get the guaranteed package to roughly $625K–$650K annualized, preferably with a meaningful sign-on.**

Because Google recruited you, you are happy at Meta, and compensation matters heavily, the burden is on Google to provide a clear switching premium—not merely match your current compensation.

## What the offer is actually worth

### Simple annualized comparison

| | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $235K |
| Target bonus | $36K | $47K |
| Annualized equity | $250K | $270K |
| **Annualized TC** | **$526K** | **$552K** |

On that basis, Google is only **$26K/year higher**, or about **5%**.

Over four years, ignoring stock appreciation, raises, and future refreshes:

- **Google:** $2.208M
- **Meta at your current $526K run rate:** $2.104M
- Difference: **$104K over four years**

That is not much compensation for taking on:

- A new manager and organization
- Performance-reset risk
- Loss of accumulated reputation and influence
- Potentially worse role/team fit
- Uncertainty around refresh grants
- The hassle and career risk of changing companies

Your next-12-month Meta compensation is apparently lower—approximately **$476K**, using the stated $200K vest—but even compared with that, the Google package is heavily affected by the vesting schedule.

### Confirm the vesting schedule before evaluating it

Google’s commonly reported new-hire schedule is front-loaded at **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, although alternate schedules exist, so the written offer controls. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

If your $1.08M grant uses 38/32/20/10, approximate TC before refreshes would be:

| Year | Equity vest | Total TC |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410.4K | **$692.4K** |
| 2 | $345.6K | **$627.6K** |
| 3 | $216K | **$498K** |
| 4 | $108K | **$390K** |

So it looks excellent in years one and two, but becomes unattractive in years three and four unless refreshes fill the gap.

Google does have an annual process that considers equity refreshes based on factors including performance, role, and location, with manager discretion—but that does not turn future refreshes into guaranteed compensation. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

**Do not value refreshes at face value when deciding.** Treat them as upside until you have actual historical data for this specific organization and level.

## Is it a lowball?

Not exactly.

Your $235K base is above the midpoint of the posted $183K–$271K range, though below your current base. Current Google Senior PM postings in the Bay Area commonly show a 20% target bonus and similarly broad base ranges. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS))

Self-reported Levels.fyi data currently puts Bay Area Google L6 Senior PM median compensation around **$551K**, almost exactly equal to this offer’s $552K annualized value. It also reports signing bonuses for PM offers, so the absence of one is negotiable rather than necessarily standard. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

Therefore:

- **As a generic Google L6 offer:** good/around market.
- **As an offer to recruit a happy Meta IC6 making $526K:** insufficient switching premium.

## What I would ask for

Make one clear, package-level counter:

- **Base:** $265,000
- **New-hire equity:** $1,400,000 over four years
- **Sign-on bonus:** $150,000

That produces recurring annualized target compensation of:

- $265K base
- $53K target bonus
- $350K annualized initial equity
- **$668K annualized TC**, plus sign-on

That is an assertive counter, but you have real leverage:

- You did not initiate the process.
- You are already at the same broad seniority level at Meta.
- You are happy and do not need to leave.
- Your current compensation is already close to the offer.
- You would be walking away from approximately $200K vesting during the next 12 months.
- Their base range extends to $271K.

They may not grant all three components, but you want to anchor high and let them tell you where flexibility exists.

### Your private target—not something to tell the recruiter

I would look for approximately:

- **Base:** at least $250K–$260K
- **Equity:** at least $1.25M–$1.35M
- **Sign-on:** at least $75K–$100K

For example:

- $250K base
- $50K bonus
- $1.3M equity, or $325K annualized
- **$625K recurring annualized TC**
- Plus a $75K–$100K sign-on

That is approximately a **19% recurring premium** over your current $526K, before the sign-on. For someone who is happy and compensation-focused, that begins to justify moving.

Do not disclose this floor.

## Suggested wording

> I’m genuinely excited about the role and the team. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking, I’m happy at Meta, and the current package is only modestly above my existing compensation on an annualized basis. I would also be walking away from approximately $200,000 of Meta equity vesting over the next 12 months.
>
> For the move to make financial sense, I’d be looking for a package closer to $265,000 in base, $1.4 million in new-hire equity, and a $150,000 sign-on bonus. I understand there may be constraints across individual components, so I’m open to how the compensation team structures it, but I would need a materially stronger guaranteed package to make the transition.

Then stop talking. Let them respond.

If the recruiter asks which component matters most:

> The overall guaranteed value matters most. My preference would be additional equity first, then base, with sign-on used to address the compensation I’m leaving behind.

Initial equity should be the priority because the recruiter has already told you refreshes are not guaranteed.

## Questions to get answered in writing

Before deciding, ask:

1. **What is the exact vesting schedule—38/32/20/10, 33/33/22/12, or something else?**
2. **When does the first vest occur?**
3. **When is the grant priced, and could the dollar value change between signing and grant approval?**
4. **Will you be eligible for the next annual refresh cycle, or will your start date cause you to miss or receive a prorated grant?**
5. **Will the first annual bonus be prorated?**
6. **When is your first performance review?**
7. **Is any sign-on repayable if you leave, and over what period?**
8. **Can the compensation team provide historical—not promised—typical refresh ranges for L6 PMs in that organization?**

The refresh-cycle eligibility question can be worth six figures over time.

## Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### My recommendation: **Negotiate**

I would not walk immediately because the initial offer is credible and Google may have substantial room. But I also would not accept it unchanged.

After negotiating:

- **Around $650K+ annualized guaranteed value plus sign-on:** strong accept, assuming you like the role.
- **Around $625K plus $75K–$100K sign-on:** reasonable accept; weigh team and career upside.
- **Around $575K–$600K with little/no sign-on:** probably stay at Meta unless the Google role is distinctly better.
- **Minimal movement from the present offer:** decline.

At the current numbers, my answer would be:

> **Good offer, but not good enough for your situation. Negotiate; if they cannot create a meaningful switching premium, stay at Meta.**

content.text:
## My recommendation: **lean yes—take it**, assuming you like the manager, team, and scope

The $200,000 sign-on changes the economics materially. The original package was close to a market match; the final package gives you a real switching premium.

### Four-year comparison

Using target compensation and ignoring stock-price changes, raises, and future refresh grants:

|  | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $240K |
| Target bonus | $36K | $48K |
| Annualized initial equity | ~$250K | $270K |
| Recurring annualized TC | **$526K** | **$558K** |
| Sign-on, annualized over 4 years | — | $50K |
| **Effective 4-year annual average** | **$526K** | **$608K** |

Four-year totals:

- **Meta at current run rate:** approximately **$2.104M**
- **Google:** approximately **$2.432M**
- **Google advantage:** approximately **$328K gross**, or **15.6%**

Because you expect only $200K of Meta RSUs in the next 12 months, Meta’s upcoming-year compensation appears to be approximately $476K. On a normalized 25%-per-year equity basis, Google would be approximately $758K in the first year including the sign-on—although actual first-year compensation depends on the written vesting schedule, start date, and bonus proration.

## What the sign-on accomplishes

Google has effectively:

1. Matched your $240K base.
2. Raised your target cash bonus by $12K annually.
3. Raised annualized initial equity by approximately $20K.
4. Replaced the $200K of Meta equity you said you were leaving behind—with cash.

That is a respectable response to your counter. The package is no longer merely “slightly more than Meta.”

The major limitation is that **only $32K of the annual advantage is recurring**:

- Google recurring TC: $558K
- Meta recurring TC: $526K
- Recurring premium: **$32K, or 6.1%**

The rest of the switching premium is the one-time sign-on. That means compensation in years three and four—and after the initial grant expires—still depends heavily on Google’s actual vesting schedule, refresh grants, promotions, and stock performance. Alphabet says its RSUs generally vest over four years and require continued employment on the applicable vesting dates. ([abc.xyz](https://abc.xyz/assets/99/21/46cafdba41089a12a2d86ea47d44/goog026-annualreport2024-web.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## When I would accept

I would take it if all of the following are true:

- You consider the Google manager credible and someone you could work for.
- The product area is reasonably stable and strategically important.
- The role has genuine L6 scope rather than an inflated title with narrower responsibilities.
- Commute and in-office expectations are acceptable.
- You are comfortable remaining through the sign-on clawback period.
- You are at least moderately enthusiastic about the work—not joining exclusively for the $200K.

You do **not** need the Google role to be clearly better than Meta. But it should be at least comparably attractive. The financial premium is meaningful enough to break a tie, but not enough to compensate for a bad manager, weak scope, or substantially worse lifestyle.

## When I would decline

Stay at Meta if:

- You have significantly more confidence in your Meta manager or promotion trajectory.
- The Google organization appears unstable or the role is poorly defined.
- You suspect you would want to return to Meta within a year.
- The work is materially less interesting.
- Google’s location or attendance requirements impose a meaningful lifestyle cost.
- You place a high value on your accumulated reputation and influence at Meta.

Put differently: **$200K is enough to justify ordinary switching risk, but not enough to ignore major role-quality concerns.**

## Confirm these terms before signing

At this stage, I would not reopen the headline compensation numbers. They have made a meaningful move and explicitly called it final. Instead, get the following details in writing.

### 1. Sign-on payment and clawback

Ask:

- When is the $200K paid?
- Is it one payment or installments?
- Is the clawback one year or two years?
- Is repayment prorated or all-or-nothing?
- Does involuntary termination without cause trigger repayment?
- Is repayment based on the **gross** amount even though you receive substantially less after withholding?

Ideally, negotiate the **clawback terms**, not the amount:

> Before I sign, could you confirm whether the sign-on repayment obligation is prorated over the applicable period and waived if employment ends involuntarily without cause?

A $200K all-or-nothing, two-year clawback is materially less attractive than a prorated one-year clawback.

The sign-on is taxable compensation. Federal withholding on separately paid supplemental wages may be 22%, but that is only withholding—not necessarily your final tax rate. At your income, you could owe more at filing, in addition to California and payroll taxes. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15?utm_source=openai))

### 2. Exact equity schedule

Do not use $270K per year unless vesting is 25% annually. Get:

- Vesting percentages by year
- First vest date
- Vesting frequency
- Grant-pricing date
- Whether the quoted $1.08M can change between acceptance and grant approval

Evaluate the offer using the schedule in your documents—not a generic schedule reported online.

### 3. First bonus

Confirm:

- Whether your first bonus is prorated
- Whether your start date makes you eligible for the next bonus cycle
- When that bonus will be paid

### 4. Refresh eligibility

Ask whether your start date makes you eligible for the **next refresh cycle**, even if prorated. You are not asking them to guarantee an award; you are confirming eligibility.

### 5. Optimize your start date

Before agreeing to a date, examine your Meta vest calendar. If you have a substantial vest coming soon, ask to begin immediately after it.

For example, moving the start date by two or three weeks to capture a $50K Meta vest could be more valuable than anything else still negotiable. Also consider whether the sign-on will be paid in 2026 or 2027; given that it is currently November 2026, the tax-year timing could matter. Consult a tax professional about your particular situation.

## Final decision

My conclusion has changed from the original offer:

- **Original offer:** negotiate or stay.
- **Final offer:** **accept, provided the role and manager are solid and the clawback terms are reasonable.**

They have given you a meaningful four-year premium, matched your base, and compensated you in cash for the Meta equity you identified. I would not reject this solely because refreshes are uncertain.

My practical standard would be:

> **If I would rate the Google opportunity at least 7/10 independent of compensation, I would accept. If the only appealing feature is the $200K sign-on, I would stay at Meta.**
